summary: Proposes a strawman position on goals and approaches for the IETF, IESG, and IAB on two related topics: supporting multiple protocols in the Internet and choosing a next-generation Internet Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1560 is the Internet Architecture Board's position paper on two big questions: how to cope with several protocol families inside the Internet, and what to do about the next version of IP. Its answer is to keep pulling everything towards one suite while making room for the others.

subtitle: The Internet Architecture Board's strawman position on protocol coexistence and on the next version of IP.

tldr.problem: The Internet was built on one protocol suite, TCP/IP, but other suites existed inside it and could not simply be ignored, while the question of what to replace IPv4 with was still open.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1560 argues from a single figure of a multiprotocol evolution process that the way to handle several suites at once is to keep converging on one primary suite while building mechanisms for interoperability and resource sharing with the others.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that specifies no standard of any kind and was offered by the IAB to stimulate discussion, with three recommendations: keep the focus on TCP/IP, pick one next-generation internet protocol, and keep exploring ways to work with other suites.

today: RFC 1560 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard of any kind, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It was prepared on behalf of the Internet Architecture Board and offered to stimulate discussion, and its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: The Question the Memo Asks
sections.content:
The memo was prepared by its authors on behalf of the Internet Architecture Board and is offered by the IAB to stimulate discussion. It takes up two topics that had recently seen considerable discussion: multiprotocol approaches in the Internet, and the selection of a next generation Internet Protocol. It suggests a strawman position for the goals and approaches of the IETF, the IESG and the IAB, and takes the view that the two topics are related, proposing directions for the three bodies to pursue.

The three directions are stated up front: maintain the focus on the TCP/IP protocol suite; work to select a single next-generation internet protocol and develop mechanisms to aid the transition from the current IPv4; and continue to explore mechanisms to interoperate and share resources with other protocol suites within the Internet.

The memo then sets out why the question is bigger than it looks. The major purpose of the Internet is to enable ubiquitous communication services between endpoints, and in a very real way the Internet is inter-enterprise networking. The issue of a multiprotocol Internet is therefore not just the issue of multiple network layers, but the issue of multiple comparable services implemented over different protocols.

It analyses the problem against two principles that hold at the same time. It is desirable to have a single protocol stack, and the community should try to avoid unconstrained proliferation of various stacks. But in reality there will always be more than one stack. The presence of multiple network layers is just one corollary of that, because even within a single stack the forces of evolution lead to periods of multiple protocols. What is needed, then, are mechanisms that maximise the services that can be provided across all the stacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB is saying that a multiprotocol Internet is not really about supporting several network layers. It is about offering the same kinds of service to people who use different protocols, and about not pretending that one stack will ever be the only one.

sections.title: The MultiProtocol Evolutionary Process
sections.content:
The picture the memo works from comes from an IAB architectural retreat held in 1991, and it describes the process of multiprotocol integration and accommodation from the point of view of a community working on a single primary protocol suite, such as the IETF, IESG and IAB working on TCP/IP. The memo notes that there is a complementary viewpoint from each of the communities whose primary focus is one of the other suites, and names IPX, OSI and SNA among them.

The existence of other protocol suites forces the community to deal with two aspects of multiprotocolism: interoperability between the primary suite and the others, and resource sharing between them. Both may happen at several levels in the protocol suites.

Achieving either is difficult, and often unanticipated interactions occur. Interoperability can be hard for reasons such as a lack of common semantics. Resource sharing can run into problems from a lack of common operational paradigms: sharing bandwidth on a link, for instance, may not work effectively if one protocol suite backs off in its demands and the other does not. Both interoperability and resource sharing require cooperation between the developers and users of the different suites. The challenge, then, is to develop mechanisms for them that have minimal negative effect on the primary protocol suite.

The memo then draws the consequence that makes the figure work. The very attempts to achieve interoperability and resource sharing lead to an attempt to bring the multiple suites into some level of harmonisation, even if only to simplify the problems of sharing and interoperability, and the communication between the communities also produces a degree of harmonisation. These processes, together with the normal process of evolution, lead to changes in the primary suite as well as the others. The need for new technologies and the need to accommodate multiple protocols therefore lead to a natural process of diversion, and the process of harmonisation leads to conversion. The same description can also be applied within the primary suite, where new technologies lead to several competing approaches, which are hoped to harmonise.
sections.plainLanguage: Making two different protocol families talk to each other, or share the same cable, forces the two communities to compromise. That compromise is what keeps the number of stacks from growing without limit, and it is also what turns one stack into a slightly different one over time.

sections.title: The Basis of the Internet
sections.content:
The memo asks why the Internet grew as it did. Some of the forces were practical, such as the bundling of TCP/IP with Berkeley Unix and the early decision to base NSFNet on TCP/IP. But the authors believe there is a more fundamental reason: the Internet, and the TCP/IP protocol suite, were targeted at inter-enterprise networking. The availability of TCP/IP on workstations, and the desire to have a single environment serve both intra- and inter-enterprise networking, led to TCP/IP being used inside organisations, but the major contribution of the Internet and TCP/IP was to give user communities the ability to communicate with other organisations and communities in a straightforward manner, using a set of common and basic services.

Fundamental to that ability was the fact that the Internet was based on a single, common, virtual network service, IP, with a supporting administrative infrastructure. That allowed a ubiquitous underlying communication infrastructure to develop, serving the global community, upon which a set of services could be provided to the user communities. It also allowed a large market to develop for application services built on the underlying communications.

An important corollary of having a single common virtual network service available to the end user is that the selection of applications becomes the province of the end-user community rather than the intermediate network provider. With a common underlying infrastructure, user communities are able to select the application services they need based on their own requirements, with the assurance that the intermediate networking service will support their communication requirements. The authors believe this has been of considerable importance in the success of the Internet.

The memo adds that IP may be used to provide network layer services for non-TCP/IP transport layers and applications. Such use is clearly beneficial, because it preserves all the benefits of a single common virtual network service while at the same time widening the set of applications available to end users.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason the Internet worked, the memo argues, is that it offered one network service to everybody. Because the network underneath was the same everywhere, people could pick whatever application they liked and be sure it would work across it.

sections.title: Directions for Multiprotocolism
sections.content:
As the scope of the Internet has grown, there has been an increasing need for mechanisms to accommodate other protocol suites. Most techniques fall into one of two categories. Interoperability techniques allow communications between users of different protocol suites. Resource sharing techniques allow common resources, such as links or switches, to jointly service communities using different protocol suites. The memo notes that such techniques have been quite limited so far, with interoperability happening primarily at the application layer and resource sharing to a limited extent.

This has led to discussion within the community about the role of the IETF, IESG and IAB with respect to the TCP/IP suite versus the other suites. Questions are asked as to whether TCP/IP is the sole domain of interest of those bodies, or whether the community needs to deal with other suites, and if so in what manner, given that those suites have their own communities of interest pursuing their own development and evolution.

The memo's answer is that the question has to be understood in the light of the process described by the figure. The continued success of the Internet relies on a continued strong force for convergence, making sure that the primary protocol suite, TCP/IP, is successful through an evolutionary process that accommodates both changing user requirements and emerging technologies. Since that process requires a continued effort to accommodate other suites within the overall Internet, efforts at interoperability and sharing must continue. The directions are therefore two-fold: have as a primary focus the evolution of the primary protocol suite, acting as a force for convergence at all times towards a single set of protocols, and make provision for other protocol suites within the global Internet through mechanisms for interoperability and resource sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer to the squabble is a division of labour. The IETF keeps TCP/IP the one suite it pushes forward, and spends the rest of its effort on making it possible for other suites to share the Internet without making TCP/IP worse.

sections.title: Selecting the Next Generation Internet Protocol
sections.content:
The same principles apply to the debate about the next generation internet protocol. There were several candidates for IPng, which raises the question of how to deal with multiple protocols at that level, and the memo notes that even if only one is selected there is an issue involved in transitioning from IPv4 to IPng.

Selecting a single Internet protocol is not the only way of dealing with the issue, the memo observes. Even if a layer of ubiquity is required, such as the one IP currently provides, ubiquity might be provided at a different layer. It might be possible to have a common transport protocol running over multiple internet protocols, or to achieve interoperability through common application services, such as directory services, running over diverse communication services at both the transport and the network layer.

These alternatives do not provide the considerable benefits of a single internet protocol and would therefore be undesirable. A single internet protocol provides a common communication infrastructure across the various networks, and that buys two things. Communities of end users can select their desired applications independently of the technologies used to support the intermediate networks. And the common underlying infrastructure provides a common marketplace upon which application developers can create new and exciting applications, whose installation does not require end users to select a corresponding network protocol, although some advanced applications may require enhancements such as high-bandwidth approaches.

So the community should continue to act as a force for convergence by selecting a single next generation Internet protocol and developing methods to ease the transition from IPv4 to IPng. Specifically, at the applications layer it is desirable to promote different approaches and let the marketplace decide. However, it is unacceptable to treat the internet protocol layer in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can safely compete with one another, because a user only has to pick the application. The network layer cannot, because two network layers cannot sit on the same wire. That is why the IAB wants one new IP and wants it chosen soon.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo ends by stating that historically the IETF, IESG and IAB have acted as a strong force for the development of the Internet by acting as a force for convergence on and evolution of a single primary protocol suite, and that this has served the community well and should be continued. The three recommendations are then repeated in full: maintain the focus on the TCP/IP protocol suite; work to select a single next-generation internet protocol and develop mechanisms to aid the transition from the current IPv4; and continue to explore mechanisms to interoperate and share resources with other protocol suites within the Internet.

The Security Considerations section is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The three recommendations come round to the same thing. Keep pushing one suite, replace IPv4 with one successor rather than several, and keep working on how other suites can share the Internet with it.
